title: Cascade Health — Security review (SOC 2, audit logs, retention, VPC/Private)
summary: Cascade Health security/compliance review covering Redwood SOC 2, audit logging, data retention controls, SSO/SAML and RBAC, encryption/KMS, and deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC). Customer requested evidence (SOC 2 report, pen test summary, subprocessors, data flow/architecture) and clarified that any PHI would require a BAA and Private/VPC deployment. Redwood outlined current controls, retention configuration, and proposed next steps: share security packet, schedule a deeper Private architecture session, and align on BAA/DPA path.
topics: Why Cascade reached out (security FAQ + VPC/private docs interest)
SOC 2 Type II scope and report sharing process
Audit logs: what events, export options, retention
Data handling: prompts/completions storage, optional logging, deletion
Encryption: in transit/at rest, KMS options, key ownership
SSO/SAML, RBAC, SCIM, and admin controls
HIPAA / BAA requirements and deployment recommendation
Private/VPC architecture overview and evidence requests
next_steps: Redwood to send Cascade the security packet (SOC 2 Type II, pen test summary letter, subprocessors list, DR/BC overview) via secure link.
Redwood to confirm current audit log event coverage and provide a sample export schema (redacted).
Schedule a 60-min Private/VPC architecture deep dive with Cascade platform team (include Ethan Park if available).
Cascade to confirm whether PHI will be processed in the initial pilot and whether a BAA is required before any production traffic.
Procurement to share Cascade’s vendor security questionnaire (SIG/CAIQ) and preferred DPA/BAA template.
action_items: Owner: Dr. Aisha Rahman — Provide SOC 2 Type II report (NDA-gated) + pen test attestation letter + subprocessors list — Due: 2025-05-16
Owner: Markus Klein — Send Private/VPC reference architecture + network requirements (VPC peering/PrivateLink options) — Due: 2025-05-16
Owner: Stephanie Nguyen — Coordinate follow-up meeting times and loop in Legal (Michael Grant) if BAA/DPA needs redlines — Due: 2025-05-15
Owner: Elena Park (Cascade) — Send vendor questionnaire and clarify PHI/BAA requirement for pilot — Due: 2025-05-19

Fireflies.ai - Call Transcript

Title: Cascade Health — Security review (SOC 2, audit logs, retention, VPC/Private)
Date: May 14, 2025
Time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 48 min
Participants:
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Dr. Aisha Rahman (Redwood Inference, Security/Privacy)
- Elena Park (Cascade Health, Security & Compliance)
- Tom Gallagher (Cascade Health, IT Director)
- Priya Desai (Cascade Health, Eng Manager)
- Megan Cho (Cascade Health, Procurement)

----

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Stephanie from Redwood Inference. I’ve got Markus, our SE, and Aisha from security with me.

[00:10] Elena Park: Hi, Elena here. Thanks for making time. We’re… we’re trying to move quickly but we have to check some boxes.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Totally understand.

[00:18] Tom Gallagher: Tom, IT. Hi.

[00:20] Priya Desai: Priya, engineering.

[00:22] Megan Cho: Megan, procurement.

[00:25] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Quick agenda from our side: understand your intended use case and what data might flow, then we can go through SOC 2, audit logs, retention, SSO, encryption, deployment options—Hosted versus VPC/Private—and leave time for evidence requests and next steps. Sound good?

[00:45] Elena Park: Yeah. And just to level set, we saw your security FAQ and the private deployment docs. We’re evaluating a couple vendors, and we need to determine if we can even do a pilot.

[00:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, makes sense. And just for context, our team flagged that you’d been looking at some of the VPC and security documentation, so we wanted to make sure we route you to the right folks instead of you waiting in a queue.

[01:08] Elena Park: Okay.

[01:09] Priya Desai: We’re building a clinician support workflow. It’s like summarizing case notes and generating draft patient messages. We have a plan to de-identify, but realistically there’s a chance PHI shows up if someone pastes a note.

[01:26] Elena Park: Which is why we’re here. If there’s PHI, we need HIPAA and we need a BAA. And we need to know if you store prompts, how long, and who can access.

[01:37] Markus Klein: Got it. That’s a key branch. Aisha can speak to our HIPAA posture and data handling, and I can go through the deployment architecture.

[01:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Hi everyone. Before I jump in, quick disclaimer: I can explain our controls and standard terms, but legal commitments like a BAA would be handled with our counsel. We do support that for the right deployment model.

[02:01] Elena Park: Understood.

[02:02] Stephanie Nguyen: And Megan, from procurement, are you mostly here for process and what docs you need?

[02:06] Megan Cho: Yes. We typically require SOC 2 Type II, a pen test summary, list of subprocessors, and our vendor security questionnaire. For HIPAA vendors we also need the BAA.

[02:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[02:20] Elena Park: Let’s start with SOC 2. Are you SOC 2 Type II and what’s the scope? Like does it cover the inference platform and the ops team.

[02:29] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, we have a current SOC 2 Type II report. Scope includes our hosted inference platform, the control plane, and supporting operations—change management, access controls, incident response, vulnerability management. It’s aligned to the Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, and Confidentiality.

[02:49] Elena Park: Can you share the report today?

[02:52] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We can share it under NDA via a secure link. If you already have an NDA with us, we can proceed; otherwise we can use our standard mutual NDA.

[03:02] Megan Cho: We don’t have an NDA executed yet.

[03:04] Stephanie Nguyen: We can send the mutual NDA right after. Usually quick.

[03:08] Elena Park: Ok. Next, audit logs. We need audit logs for admin actions and access, and preferably API usage logs. What do you provide and what’s the retention.

[03:20] Markus Klein: So there are a couple layers. In the Redwood Console, we have audit logging for organization and workspace actions—like user invites, role changes, API key creation/rotation, SSO configuration changes, model deployment config changes if you’re in Dedicated/Private. Then we have request-level telemetry—latency, tokens, error codes—that can be configured.

[03:44] Elena Park: Request-level telemetry meaning prompts are stored?

[03:47] Markus Klein: Not necessarily. By default for Hosted API we log metadata for billing and reliability—like token counts, timestamps, model, region, status codes. Prompt and completion logging is configurable. Many customers keep content logging off.

[04:04] Dr. Aisha Rahman: To be precise, we separate content from metadata. Content retention is opt-in for debugging/evals, and can be disabled. For regulated workloads we recommend keeping content logging disabled and using Private deployment where feasible.

[04:19] Elena Park: When you say “can be disabled,” is it truly disabled? Like not in any logs, not in S3, not in support tools.

[04:26] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Correct. When disabled, we do not persist prompt/completion bodies in our standard logging pipeline. There are still transient in-memory processing steps, but no durable storage of content. We can provide our data handling document that describes that.

[04:42] Tom Gallagher: So the metadata logs—how long do you keep those.

[04:46] Markus Klein: Standard retention in Console varies by plan. For enterprise we can configure longer retention for audit logs, and also export to your SIEM. A lot of teams send audit logs to Splunk or Datadog.

[04:59] Elena Park: What’s “enterprise” in this context. We’re on self-serve right now.

[05:03] Stephanie Nguyen: Yeah, so self-serve hosted has the basics, and Dedicated/Private is where we get into custom retention, private networking, and contractual controls.

[05:12] Elena Park: Okay but we can’t move forward if we can’t get audit logs exported, at least for admin actions.

[05:18] Markus Klein: Understood. For Dedicated and Private, audit log export is a standard requirement; we can do webhook export or periodic export depending on the integration. We can confirm the exact mechanism you prefer.

[05:30] Priya Desai: What about model outputs. If we do a Private deployment, does Redwood still have access.

[05:35] Markus Klein: In a Private deployment—VPC model—you have a private control plane and customer-managed networking. Redwood operators have highly restricted access, and access is logged and time-bound. In some variants, the data plane runs in your VPC with no public ingress.

[05:52] Elena Park: That’s the direction we’d want.

[05:54] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And from a compliance standpoint, Private is the recommended path for PHI. Dedicated can also be appropriate depending on the exact terms and isolation requirements, but for HIPAA conversations we typically steer to Private.

[06:08] Megan Cho: So HIPAA—do you sign BAAs.

[06:11] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We do for eligible customers, generally tied to Private deployments and specific operational controls. Legal will confirm specifics. We’ll need to understand the data types and whether it’s production PHI.

[06:25] Elena Park: Let’s talk retention and deletion. We have requirements around deletion within 30 days of request and minimum retention. How do you handle that.

[06:35] Dr. Aisha Rahman: For content that is persisted—again, only if enabled—we support deletion requests and can purge associated records. For metadata we retain for billing and security; in Private deployments we can align retention windows contractually and technically, including customer-controlled retention for certain logs. We also document our retention policy and you can set stricter settings.

[06:56] Priya Desai: But like, if a user asks us “delete all my data,” are we blocked by your retention.

[07:02] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Typically, your application data should not be stored by us if you disable content logging. In that case the delete request is mostly on your side. For logs, metadata may persist for a defined period. If you need strict deletion semantics, Private with customer-managed storage/logging is the best fit.

[07:20] Elena Park: Okay. Encryption. Is everything encrypted at rest and in transit. Do you support customer-managed keys.

[07:28] Markus Klein: TLS in transit. At rest encryption in our managed services. For Private, we can integrate with cloud KMS—customer-managed keys for certain storage components depending on the architecture.

[07:40] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And access to keys is controlled by your cloud policies if we’re integrating into your KMS. For hosted, keys are managed by Redwood.

[07:49] Tom Gallagher: Do you have SSO. SAML.

[07:51] Markus Klein: Yes. SSO/SAML for enterprise plans, plus RBAC roles at org/workspace level. Also SCIM is available for provisioning in those tiers.

[08:01] Elena Park: Is RBAC granular enough. We need separation between developers and security admins.

[08:07] Markus Klein: We have roles like org admin, billing admin, developer, read-only, and you can scope access per workspace. For the exact matrix, we can send the RBAC doc.

[08:19] Elena Park: Good.

[08:20] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to pause and make sure we’re tracking what you need. Elena, what are the “must have” items to approve a pilot.

[08:28] Elena Park: Must have: SOC 2 Type II, pen test evidence, subprocessors, and a clear statement on whether prompts are stored and how to disable. Also for any PHI, we need BAA. If you can’t do BAA we can maybe do a de-identified pilot, but we have to prove it.

[08:46] Priya Desai: And network-wise, we can’t call a public endpoint from certain environments. We’d need private connectivity or at least allowlisting and no public internet egress.

[08:57] Markus Klein: That’s exactly what Private/VPC addresses. There are a couple connectivity patterns: VPC peering, PrivateLink-type endpoints depending on cloud, or customer-managed ingress. We can get specific based on where you run—AWS, Azure.

[09:11] Priya Desai: We’re AWS.

[09:12] Markus Klein: Great.

[09:14] Elena Park: Also: do you use subcontractors for processing. Like do you send data to OpenAI or something.

[09:19] Markus Klein: No, we run inference on our infrastructure and do not forward your prompts to third-party model APIs unless you explicitly configure a third-party endpoint, which is not what we’re discussing here.

[09:33] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Our subprocessors are primarily infrastructure and tooling providers—cloud providers, monitoring, support systems. We maintain a published subprocessors list, and we can provide it.

[09:44] Elena Park: Okay.

[09:46] Megan Cho: For the pen test, do you have a full report or a letter.

[09:50] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We typically provide an attestation letter and executive summary, and under NDA we can provide more detail. Full raw reports sometimes have sensitive exploit details; we handle case-by-case.

[10:03] Megan Cho: That’s fine.

[10:05] Elena Park: Incident response. Do you have a defined SLA for notification.

[10:10] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes. Our security incident response process includes customer notification timelines aligned with contractual terms. For enterprise contracts we can define notification windows.

[10:23] Tom Gallagher: Data residency. We’re US only today but we might expand.

[10:27] Markus Klein: We can run in multiple regions. For Private you can pick the region, and we can keep data plane in-region.

[10:35] Elena Park: What about support access. We’ve had issues with vendors where support can just hop in.

[10:41] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Support access is controlled. For Private deployments, access to systems is via audited, time-bound mechanisms with approvals, and we can align on break-glass procedures. For hosted, access is still restricted and logged.

[10:57] Priya Desai: Can you show what audit logs look like.

[11:00] Markus Klein: I don’t have the console open on this call, but we can provide a sample schema. It’s basically event type, actor, timestamp, target resource, and source IP where applicable.

[11:12] Elena Park: Please do.

[11:13] Stephanie Nguyen: Aisha, can you speak to data retention in practical terms. Like if they disable content logging, what’s still present.

[11:22] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Sure. If content logging is disabled: we retain operational metadata required for billing and service reliability—counts, timings, error codes, model identifiers, and routing/region. We do not store prompt or completion bodies. For Dedicated/Private, we can set additional controls so even metadata logging is tuned to minimum necessary, and provide options to export to your own storage.

[11:49] Elena Park: And backups? Sometimes vendors say they delete but it’s in backups.

[11:53] Dr. Aisha Rahman: For systems where content could be stored (when enabled), our deletion process includes purging from primary storage and handling within backup retention cycles according to our policy. For regulated workloads, again, the recommendation is not to store content in the first place, and for Private to use customer-controlled storage.

[12:15] Elena Park: Okay. That’s the right answer.

[12:17] (crosstalk)

[12:18] Tom Gallagher: Sorry, one more. Key rotation. API keys. Can we rotate and do you have audit events.

[12:24] Markus Klein: Yes. You can create and rotate API keys, and those actions generate audit events.

[12:31] Elena Park: Good.

[12:33] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we talk about deployment options for a second. Today you’re on self-serve hosted, right?

[12:39] Priya Desai: We signed up with a card to test. It’s not in production.

[12:43] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. For a HIPAA-adjacent evaluation, we’d likely propose a Private pilot in AWS region that works for you, with private networking. That’s a sales-assisted motion. You can still do quick testing on hosted for non-sensitive data.

[13:00] Elena Park: What’s the lead time.

[13:02] Markus Klein: Depends on complexity. A basic Private/VPC setup can be a few weeks, but networking and security reviews can extend it. For a proof-of-concept, we can also do Dedicated with strict settings, but for PHI, Private is better.

[13:18] Elena Park: Our internal timeline is 6 weeks to have something in front of clinicians.

[13:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, that’s helpful.

[13:25] Megan Cho: We will need the vendor questionnaire done within two weeks or procurement will block.

[13:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it.

[13:32] Elena Park: Let’s go through evidence list. I’ll read and you tell me yes/no. SOC 2 Type II.

[13:38] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, NDA.

[13:40] Elena Park: Pen test.

[13:41] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, summary/letter.

[13:43] Elena Park: Subprocessors list.

[13:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes.

[13:46] Elena Park: Data flow diagram.

[13:48] Markus Klein: We have a reference architecture and data flow for Hosted and for Private. We can share those.

[13:55] Elena Park: Good. DR/BC plan.

[13:58] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We can share an overview. Detailed internal runbooks are not shared, but we share RTO/RPO targets and the process.

[14:06] Elena Park: That’s fine.

[14:08] Elena Park: Also, we need to know if you support customer-managed keys.

[14:12] Markus Klein: For Private, yes, we can integrate with your AWS KMS for specific components. We’ll document what’s supported in the architecture.

[14:20] Elena Park: Okay.

[14:21] Priya Desai: Question on logging. Our clinicians might generate problematic prompts. We need to be able to investigate. If you don’t store prompts, how do we debug.

[14:32] Markus Klein: Common pattern is you log prompts in your own system under your controls, then send only what’s needed to Redwood. Or you enable short-term content logging in a sandbox with strict access and short retention. But in regulated settings, most customers keep content in their own environment.

[14:52] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[14:54] Elena Park: Another question: access control for your employees. Is it least privilege. Do you do background checks.

[15:01] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes. We enforce least privilege, role-based access, MFA, and regular access reviews. Employee security training is mandatory; background checks are conducted for roles with elevated access. Details are in our SOC 2 controls and we can provide a security overview.

[15:18] Elena Park: Great.

[15:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Elena, you mentioned evaluating other vendors. Without naming names, what are you comparing.

[15:26] Elena Park: We’re looking at… AWS Bedrock because it’s already in our AWS account. Also Azure OpenAI came up. And a couple “LLM API” vendors. Our main concern is control and auditability.

[15:39] Markus Klein: Understood. Our differentiation is the deployment flexibility and inference controls. Private gives you isolation plus predictable performance.

[15:49] Priya Desai: Performance is important too but this call is mostly security.

[15:52] Markus Klein: Yep.

[15:54] Elena Park: For VPC deployment, do you require inbound connectivity from your side. Like do you need to connect into our VPC.

[16:01] Markus Klein: Usually it’s the other way around: your app connects to a private endpoint. Depending on the architecture, the inference service runs in a dedicated environment with private routing. We’ll go into detail in the follow-up.

[16:15] Tom Gallagher: If it’s in our VPC, who patches it.

[16:18] Markus Klein: For Private, Redwood manages the platform components as part of the service, but you control the networking perimeter. There are variants where it’s more customer-managed; again, we’ll scope what you want.

[16:32] Elena Park: Okay.

[16:34] Megan Cho: Do you have any ISO certifications.

[16:37] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Not at this time; we rely on SOC 2 Type II as the primary attestation. Some customers accept that.

[16:45] Megan Cho: Okay.

[16:47] Elena Park: Data classification. Do you support tagging data.

[16:51] Markus Klein: Not directly as “classification” in the API, but you can route workloads per workspace and configure logging/retention per workspace in enterprise tiers. Some teams map workspaces to data classes.

[17:06] Elena Park: Good.

[17:08] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to make sure we’re not missing anything. Elena, any other requirements like FedRAMP, HITRUST.

[17:14] Elena Park: We are not FedRAMP. HITRUST is a plus but not required. HIPAA is the key.

[17:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Understood.

[17:22] Priya Desai: So what do we need to do to get a Private pilot started.

[17:27] Stephanie Nguyen: We typically do: a short technical scoping call for networking + throughput, then we send an order form and kick off provisioning. In parallel we run security/procurement workstream. Markus can lead the technical scoping.

[17:42] Markus Klein: And we’ll define what model(s), expected tokens per day, latency targets, and any special requirements like deterministic routing, fallbacks, etc.

[17:53] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:55] Elena Park: One more question. Do you support audit logs for model changes. Like if you change model versions.

[18:02] Markus Klein: Yes. Model version pinning and rollouts are part of the platform; changes are logged in audit events. For Private, you can pin a version and control canary/fallback.

[18:15] Elena Park: Good.

[18:17] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And we can provide change management evidence in the SOC report. It covers our SDLC controls.

[18:24] Elena Park: Okay.

[18:26] (pause)

[18:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Should we talk about how we handle PHI specifically. Aisha.

[18:32] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Sure. We do not market ourselves as “HIPAA compliant out of the box” on the self-serve hosted tier. If you anticipate PHI, we recommend Private with contractual safeguards, access controls, and a BAA if required. You should also implement application-level safeguards—redaction where possible, minimum necessary data, and user training.

[18:58] Elena Park: That aligns with our policy.

[19:00] Megan Cho: We’ll need the BAA template. Or you need ours.

[19:03] Stephanie Nguyen: We can start with our standard and compare. If you have a standard, send it.

[19:08] Megan Cho: Okay.

[19:10] Priya Desai: Is there a way to block certain content types. Like if a prompt contains MRN.

[19:16] Markus Klein: We don’t have built-in DLP in the inference API today. Many customers use upstream DLP filters or policy engines. Some do regex-based checks, others use dedicated DLP tools.

[19:30] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:32] Elena Park: We also need to know your support hours, and on-call.

[19:36] Stephanie Nguyen: For Private and enterprise tiers, we have SLA-backed support and defined response times. We can share the support policy.

[19:45] Elena Park: Great.

[19:47] (minor audio glitch)

[19:49] Elena Park: Sorry, you cut out. Did you say SLA backed.

[19:52] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, SLA-backed support for those tiers.

[19:55] Elena Park: Okay.

[19:57] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s recap what we’ll send. Aisha: SOC 2 under NDA, pen test summary, subprocessors list, DR/BC overview. Markus: audit log schema and Private architecture, network requirements. And we’ll set up a technical deep dive.

[20:15] Markus Klein: Yep.

[20:16] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes.

[20:18] Elena Park: That’s good. Also, our questionnaire. I’ll send it.

[20:22] Megan Cho: I’ll coordinate with Elena on that.

[20:25] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Before we close, any blockers you foresee.

[20:30] Elena Park: Honestly the biggest blocker is BAA. If you can’t sign, we can’t do PHI. If we can do a de-identified pilot without PHI, maybe, but engineering needs to be comfortable.

[20:42] Priya Desai: We can do a de-identified dataset for evaluation. But real-world usage is messy.

[20:48] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Understood. We’ll bring in legal early so it doesn’t surprise anyone.

[20:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[20:56] Markus Klein: And for the Private deep dive, we’ll cover connectivity, isolation, and how logs flow to you.

[21:02] Tom Gallagher: Please include your networking person.

[21:05] Stephanie Nguyen: We can include Ethan Park from platform/control plane integration, if he’s available.

[21:10] Elena Park: Great.

[21:12] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, I’ll send a follow-up email today with the NDA and proposed times. Thanks everyone.

[21:18] Elena Park: Thanks.

[21:19] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[21:20] Megan Cho: Thank you.

[21:22] Tom Gallagher: Bye.

----

Auto-generated Notes (Fireflies)
- Key Questions:
  - Does Redwood store prompt/completion content, and can it be disabled?
  - What audit logs are available and can they be exported?
  - Can Redwood support Private/VPC deployment in AWS with private connectivity?
  - What evidence can Redwood provide (SOC 2, pen test, DR/BC, subprocessors)?
  - Is a BAA available for PHI workloads?

- Risks flagged:
  - PHI/BAA requirement may gate pilot.
  - Public endpoint restrictions (needs private connectivity).

- Decisions:
  - Proceed with NDA + evidence packet.
  - Schedule Private/VPC architecture deep dive.
